a1_answer:
PROPOSED DESIGN INTERVENTION: Dynamic Balancing Pulse Modulation adjusts the duty cycle of the existing 1 A passive balancer in real-time. The controller prioritizes energy extraction from hot cells to prevent capacity loss and self-discharge drift. This maintains the 35 mV rest voltage spread without increasing module footprint.

MECHANISM: Self-discharge and capacity fade accelerate in hot cells due to accelerated side-reaction kinetics. The inverted pulse logic extracts charge from high-temperature cells, where self-discharge is higher, and deposits it into low-temperature cells, which retain charge longer. This reduces the net voltage spread caused by thermal gradients and asymmetric self-discharge rates.

DEPARTURE FROM STANDARD: Standard balancers use fixed pulse widths or symmetric balancing, which fails under 15 C gradients. This design inverts the pulse direction to prioritize hot cells, directly countering the specific failure mode of thermal-driven self-discharge asymmetry.

LABELED PARAMETERS:
ASSUMPTION PARAMETER: Max cell-to-cell voltage spread = 35 mV (User Constraint; target limit)
ASSUMPTION PARAMETER: Thermal gradient = 15 C (User Constraint; top-to-bottom module differential)
ASSUMPTION PARAMETER: Balancing current = 1 A (User Constraint; existing hardware limit)
ASSUMPTION PARAMETER: Calendar life = 10 years (User Constraint; service requirement)
ASSUMPTION PARAMETER: Pulse duration = 10 ms (Design choice; minimum effective duty cycle for measurable correction). Engineering basis: The 10 ms duration is selected based on the RC time constant of the cell's internal impedance to ensure the pulse is short enough to minimize resistive heating while long enough to overcome switch propagation delays in the existing 1 A balancer topology. Calibration path: The duration is calibrated via sensitivity analysis of temperature rise versus pulse width at 45 C ambient, ensuring ΔT < 0.1 C per pulse to maintain thermal neutrality [doi:10.1016/j.est.2024.112224].
ASSUMPTION PARAMETER: Pulse charge transfer = 0.00278 mAh per 10 ms pulse (Calculated: 1 A × 0.01 s / 3600 s/hour). Engineering basis: This value is derived strictly from the physical constraints of the 1 A hardware limit and the selected 10 ms duration. It represents the theoretical maximum charge per pulse. Sensitivity path: Actual effective transfer is lower due to switch inefficiency and parasitic resistance; this value serves as the upper bound for duty cycle calculation, with a 15% derating factor applied in final control loops to account for non-idealities [doi:10.1016/j.est.2024.112224].
ASSUMPTION PARAMETER: NMC cathode structure = layered LiNi_x Mn_y Co_z O_2 [doi:10.1021/jacs.5c15171] — (Confirms material chemistry underlying self-discharge kinetics). Engineering basis: NMC-811 is selected due to its high specific energy and well-characterized self-discharge behavior under thermal stress, which is critical for the 15 C gradient scenario. The layered structure allows for predictable Li-ion diffusion coefficients, enabling accurate modeling of the self-discharge rate differential between hot and cold cells. Calibration path: The chemical kinetic parameters (activation energy for side reactions) are calibrated against empirical self-discharge data from NMC-811 cells at 45 C and 25 C to refine the control model [doi:10.1021/jacs.5c15171, doi:10.1016/j.fub.2026.100159].

FALSIFICATION TEST: Subject 13-cell NMC-811 modules (n = 5 independent units) to a 15 C top-to-bottom thermal gradient at 45 C ambient. Apply dynamic pulse modulation for 10 years. Measure cell-to-cell voltage spread at rest. Pass if spread remains below 35 mV.
